\NeedsTeXFormat{LaTeX2e}
\ProvidesClass{iopart}[1996/06/10 v0.0 IOP Journals LaTeX article class]
\newcommand\@ptsize{0}
\newif\if@restonecol
\newif\if@titlepage
\newif\ifiopams
\@titlepagefalse
\DeclareOption{a4paper}
   {\setlength\paperheight {297mm}%
    \setlength\paperwidth  {210mm}}
\DeclareOption{letterpaper}
   {\setlength\paperheight {11in}%
    \setlength\paperwidth  {8.5in}}
\DeclareOption{landscape}
   {\setlength\@tempdima   {\paperheight}%
    \setlength\paperheight {\paperwidth}%
    \setlength\paperwidth  {\@tempdima}}
\DeclareOption{10pt}{\renewcommand\@ptsize{0}}
\DeclareOption{11pt}{\renewcommand\@ptsize{2}} % No 11pt version
\DeclareOption{12pt}{\renewcommand\@ptsize{2}}
\DeclareOption{draft}{\setlength\overfullrule{5pt}}
\DeclareOption{final}{\setlength\overfullrule{0pt}}
\DeclareOption{titlepage}{\@titlepagetrue}
\DeclareOption{notitlepage}{\@titlepagefalse}
\ExecuteOptions{letterpaper,final}
\ProcessOptions
\DeclareMathAlphabet{\bi}{OML}{cmm}{b}{it}
\DeclareMathAlphabet{\bcal}{OMS}{cmsy}{b}{n}

\setlength\normallineskip{1\p@}

\@highpenalty 301
\setlength\parindent{2em}

\setcounter{bottomnumber}{3}

\setcounter{totalnumber}{8}

%
\pretolerance=5000
\tolerance=8000
%
% Headings for all pages apart from first
%
\def\ps@headings{\let\@oddfoot\@empty
      \let\@evenfoot\@empty
      \def\@evenhead{\thepage\hfil\itshape\rightmark}%
      \def\@oddhead{{\itshape\leftmark}\hfil\thepage}%
      \let\@mkboth\markboth
      \let\sectionmark\@gobble
      \let\subsectionmark\@gobble}
%
% Headings for first page
%
\def\ps@myheadings{\let\@oddfoot\@empty\let\@evenfoot\@empty
    \let\@oddhead\@empty\let\@evenhead\@empty
    \let\@mkboth\@gobbletwo
    \let\sectionmark\@gobble
    \let\subsectionmark\@gobble}
%
% \maketitle just ends page
%
\newcommand\maketitle{\newpage}
%
% Article titles
%
% Usage: \title[Short title]{Full title}
% [Short title] is optional; use where title is too long
% or contains footnotes, 50 characters maximum 
%
\renewcommand{\title}{\@ifnextchar[{\@stitle}{\@ftitle}}
\def\@stitle[#1]#2{\markboth{#1}{#1}%
    \thispagestyle{myheadings}%
    \vspace*{3pc}{\exhyphenpenalty=10000\hyphenpenalty=10000 
    \Large\raggedright\noindent
    \bf#2\par}}
\def\@ftitle#1{\markboth{#1}{#1}%
    \thispagestyle{myheadings}%
    \vspace*{3pc}{\exhyphenpenalty=10000\hyphenpenalty=10000 
    \Large\raggedright\noindent
    \bf#1\par}}
%
% Can use \paper instead of \title
%
\let\paper=\title
%
% Generic title command for articles other than papers
%
% Usage: \article[Short title]{Article Type}{Full title}
% [Short title] is optional; use where title is too long
% or contains footnotes, 50 characters maximum 
%
\newcommand{\article}{\@ifnextchar[{\@sarticle}{\@farticle}}
\def\@sarticle[#1]#2#3{\markboth{#1}{#1}%
    \thispagestyle{myheadings}%
     \vspace*{.5pc}%
    {\parindent=\mathindent \bf #2\par}%
     \vspace*{1.5pc}%
    {\exhyphenpenalty=10000\hyphenpenalty=10000
     \Large\raggedright\noindent
     \bf#3\par}}%
\def\@farticle#1#2{\markboth{#2}{#2}%
    \thispagestyle{myheadings}%
     \vspace*{.5pc}%
    {\parindent=\mathindent \bf #1\par}%
     \vspace*{1.5pc}%
    {\exhyphenpenalty=10000\hyphenpenalty=10000
     \Large\raggedright\noindent
     \bf#2\par}}%
%
% Letters to the Editor
%
% Usage \letter{Full title}
% No short title is required for Letters
%
\def\letter#1{\article[Letter to the Editor]{Letter to the Editor}{#1}}
%
% Fast Track Communications (added by sxb 9 March 2011)
%
% Usage \ftc{Full title} - there's no short title
\def\ftc#1{\article[Fast Track Communication]{Fast Track Communication}{#1}}
%
%
% Review articles
%
% Usage: \review[Short title]{Full title}
% [Short title] is optional; use where title is too long
% or contains footnotes, 50 characters maximum 
%
\def\review{\@ifnextchar[{\@sreview}{\@freview}}
\def\@sreview[#1]#2{\@sarticle[#1]{Review Article}{#2}}
\def\@freview#1{\@farticle{Review Article}{#1}}
%
% Topical Review
%
% Usage: \topical[Short title]{Full title}
% [Short title] is optional; use where title is too long
% or contains footnotes, 50 characters maximum 
%
\def\topical{\@ifnextchar[{\@stopical}{\@ftopical}}
\def\@stopical[#1]#2{\@sarticle[#1]{Topical Review}{#2}}
\def\@ftopical#1{\@farticle{Topical Review}{#1}}
%
% Comments
%
% Usage: \comment[Short title]{Full title}
% [Short title] is optional; use where title is too long
% or contains footnotes, 50 characters maximum 
%
\def\comment{\@ifnextchar[{\@scomment}{\@fcomment}}
\def\@scomment[#1]#2{\@sarticle[#1]{Comment}{#2}}
\def\@fcomment#1{\@farticle{Comment}{#1}}
%
% Rapid Communications
%
% Usage: \rapid[Short title]{Full title}
% [Short title] is optional; use where title is too long
% or contains footnotes, 50 characters maximum 
%
\def\rapid{\@ifnextchar[{\@srapid}{\@frapid}}
\def\@srapid[#1]#2{\@sarticle[#1]{Rapid Communication}{#2}}
\def\@frapid#1{\@farticle{Rapid Communication}{#1}}
%
% Notes
%
% Usage: \note[Short title]{Full title}
% [Short title] is optional; use where title is too long
% or contains footnotes, 50 characters maximum 
%
\def\note{\@ifnextchar[{\@snote}{\@fnote}}
\def\@snote[#1]#2{\@sarticle[#1]{Note}{#2}}
\def\@fnote#1{\@farticle{Note}{#1}}
%
% Preliminary Communications
%
% Usage: \prelim[Short title]{Full title}
% [Short title] is optional; use where title is too long
% or contains footnotes, 50 characters maximum 
%
\def\prelim{\@ifnextchar[{\@sprelim}{\@fprelim}}
\def\@sprelim[#1]#2{\@sarticle[#1]{Preliminary Communication}{#2}}
\def\@fprelim#1{\@farticle{Preliminary Communication}{#1}}
%
% List of authors
%
% Usage \author[Short form]{List of all authors}
% The short form excludes footnote symbols linking authors to addresses 
% and is used for running heads in printed version (but not on preprints)
%
\renewcommand{\author}{\@ifnextchar[{\@sauthor}{\@fauthor}}
\def\@sauthor[#1]#2{\markright{#1}    % for production only
   \vspace*{1.5pc}%
   \begin{indented}%
   \item[]\normalsize\bf\raggedright#2
   \end{indented}%
   \smallskip}
\def\@fauthor#1{%\markright{#1}         for production only
   \vspace*{1.5pc}%
   \begin{indented}%
   \item[]\normalsize\bf\raggedright#1
   \end{indented}%
   \smallskip}
%
% Affiliation (authors address)
%
% Usage: \address{Address of first author}
%        \address{Address of second author}
% Use once for each address, use symbols \dag \ddag \S \P $\|$
% to connect authors with addresses
%
\newcommand{\address}[1]{\begin{indented}
   \item[]\rm\raggedright #1
   \end{indented}}
%
% American Mathematical Society Classification Numbers
% Usage: \ams{57.XX, 58.XX}
%
\def\ams#1{\vspace{10pt}
     \begin{indented}
     \item[]\rm AMS classification scheme numbers: #1\par
     \end{indented}}
%
% A single Physics & Astronomy Classification Number
% Usage \pacno{31.10}
%
\def\pacno#1{\vspace{10pt}
     \begin{indented}
     \item[]\rm PACS number: #1\par
     \end{indented}}
%
% Physics & Astronomy Classification Numbers (more than one)
% Usage \pacs{31.10, 31.20T}
%
\def\pacs#1{\vspace{10pt}
     \begin{indented}
     \item[]\rm PACS numbers: #1\par
     \end{indented}}
%
% Submission details. If \jl command used journals name printed
% otherwise Institute of Physics Publishing 
%
\def\submitted{\vspace{28pt plus 10pt minus 18pt}
     \noindent{\small\rm Submitted to: {\it \journal}\par}}
%
\def\submitto#1{\vspace{28pt plus 10pt minus 18pt}
     \noindent{\small\rm Submitted to: {\it #1}\par}}
%
% For articles (other than Letters) not divided into sections
% Usage \nosections Start of text
%
\def\nosections{\vspace{30\p@ plus12\p@ minus12\p@}
    \noindent\ignorespaces}
%
% Acknowledgments (no heading if letter)
% Usage \ack for Acknowledgments, \ackn for Acknowledgement
%
\def\ack{\ifletter\bigskip\noindent\ignorespaces\else
    \section*{Acknowledgments}\fi}
\def\ackn{\ifletter\bigskip\noindent\ignorespaces\else
    \section*{Acknowledgment}\fi}
%
% Footnotes: symbols selected in order \dag (1), \ddag (2), \S (3), 
% $\|$ (4), $\P$ (5), $^+$ (6), $^*$ (7), \sharp (8), \dagger\dagger (9)
% unless optional argument of [<num>] use to specify required symbol, 
% 1=\dag, 2=\ddag, etc
% Usage: \footnote{Text of footnote}
%        \footnote[3]{Text of footnote}
%
\def\footnoterule{}%
\setcounter{footnote}{1}
\long\def\@makefntext#1{\parindent 1em\noindent 
 \makebox[1em][l]{\footnotesize\rm$\m@th{\fnsymbol{footnote}}$}%
 \footnotesize\rm #1}
\def\@makefnmark{\hbox{${\fnsymbol{footnote}}\m@th$}}
\def\@thefnmark{\fnsymbol{footnote}}
\def\footnote{\@ifnextchar[{\@xfootnote}{\stepcounter{\@mpfn}%
       \begingroup\let\protect\noexpand
       \xdef\@thefnmark{\thempfn}\endgroup
     \@footnotemark\@footnotetext}}
\def\@xfootnote[#1]{\setcounter{footnote}{#1}%
   \addtocounter{footnote}{-1}\footnote}
\def\@fnsymbol#1{\ifcase#1\or \dagger\or \ddagger\or \S\or
   \|\or \P\or ^{+}\or ^{\tsty *}\or \sharp
   \or \dagger\dagger \else\@ctrerr\fi\relax}

% E-mail addresses (to provide links from headers)

\def\eads#1{\vspace*{5pt}\address{E-mail: #1}}

%
% Switches

\newif\ifletter

\setcounter{secnumdepth}{3}
\newcounter {section}
\newcounter {subsection}[section]
\newcounter {subsubsection}[subsection]
\newcounter {paragraph}[subsubsection]
\newcounter {subparagraph}[paragraph]
\renewcommand\thesection       {\arabic{section}}
\renewcommand\thesubsection    {\thesection.\arabic{subsection}}
\renewcommand\thesubsubsection {\thesubsection.\arabic{subsubsection}}
\renewcommand\theparagraph     {\thesubsubsection.\arabic{paragraph}}
\renewcommand\thesubparagraph  {\theparagraph.\arabic{subparagraph}}
\def\@chapapp{Section}

\newcommand\section{\@startsection {section}{1}{\z@}%
                   {-3.5ex \@plus -1ex \@minus -.2ex}%
                   {2.3ex \@plus.2ex}%
                   {\reset@font\normalsize\bfseries\raggedright}}
\newcommand\subsection{\@startsection{subsection}{2}{\z@}%
                   {-3.25ex\@plus -1ex \@minus -.2ex}%
                   {1.5ex \@plus .2ex}%
                   {\reset@font\normalsize\itshape\raggedright}}
\newcommand\subsubsection{\@startsection{subsubsection}{3}{\z@}%
                                     {-3.25ex\@plus -1ex \@minus -.2ex}%
                                     {-1em \@plus .2em}%
                                     {\reset@font\normalsize\itshape}}
\newcommand\paragraph{\@startsection{paragraph}{4}{\z@}%
                                    {3.25ex \@plus1ex \@minus.2ex}%
                                    {-1em}%
                                    {\reset@font\normalsize\itshape}}
\newcommand\subparagraph{\@startsection{subparagraph}{5}{\parindent}%
                                       {3.25ex \@plus1ex \@minus .2ex}%
                                       {-1em}%
                                      {\reset@font\normalsize\itshape}}
\def\@sect#1#2#3#4#5#6[#7]#8{\ifnum #2>\c@secnumdepth
     \let\@svsec\@empty\else
     \refstepcounter{#1}\edef\@svsec{\csname the#1\endcsname. }\fi
     \@tempskipa #5\relax
      \ifdim \@tempskipa>\z@
        \begingroup #6\relax
          \noindent{\hskip #3\relax\@svsec}{\interlinepenalty \@M #8\par}%
        \endgroup
       \csname #1mark\endcsname{#7}\addcontentsline
         {toc}{#1}{\ifnum #2>\c@secnumdepth \else
                      \protect\numberline{\csname the#1\endcsname}\fi
                    #7}\else
        \def\@svsechd{#6\hskip #3\relax  %% \relax added 2 May 90
                   \@svsec #8\csname #1mark\endcsname
                      {#7}\addcontentsline
                           {toc}{#1}{\ifnum #2>\c@secnumdepth \else
                             \protect\numberline{\csname the#1\endcsname}\fi
                       #7}}\fi
     \@xsect{#5}}
%
\def\@ssect#1#2#3#4#5{\@tempskipa #3\relax
   \ifdim \@tempskipa>\z@
     \begingroup #4\noindent{\hskip #1}{\interlinepenalty \@M #5\par}\endgroup
   \else \def\@svsechd{#4\hskip #1\relax #5}\fi
    \@xsect{#3}}

\newenvironment{abstract}{%
      \vspace{16pt plus3pt minus3pt}
      \begin{indented}
      \item[]{\bfseries \abstractname.}\quad\rm\ignorespaces} 
      {\end{indented}\if@titlepage\newpage\else\vspace{18\p@ plus18\p@}\fi}
\newenvironment{verse}
               {\let\\=\@centercr
                \list{}{\itemsep      \z@
                        \itemindent   -1.5em%
                        \listparindent\itemindent
                        \rightmargin  \leftmargin
                        \advance\leftmargin 1.5em}%
                \item[]}
               {\endlist}
\newenvironment{quotation}
               {\list{}{\listparindent 1.5em%
                        \itemindent    \listparindent
                        \rightmargin   \leftmargin
                        \parsep        \z@ \@plus\p@}%
                \item[]}
               {\endlist}
\newenvironment{quote}
               {\list{}{\rightmargin\leftmargin}%
                \item[]}
               {\endlist}
\newenvironment{titlepage}
    {%
        \@restonecolfalse\newpage
      \thispagestyle{empty}%
      \if@compatibility
        \setcounter{page}{0}
      \else
        \setcounter{page}{1}%
      \fi}%
    {\newpage\setcounter{page}{1}}
\def\appendix{\@ifnextchar*{\@appendixstar}{\@appendix}}
\def\@appendix{\eqnobysec\@appendixstar}
\def\@appendixstar{\@@par
 \ifnumbysec                         %  Added 30/4/94 to get Table A1,
 \@addtoreset{table}{section}        %  Table B1 etc if numbering by
 \@addtoreset{figure}{section}\fi    %  section
 \setcounter{section}{0}
 \setcounter{subsection}{0}
 \setcounter{subsubsection}{0}
 \setcounter{equation}{0}
 \setcounter{figure}{0}
 \setcounter{table}{0}
 \def\thesection{Appendix \Alph{section}}   
 \def\theequation{\ifnumbysec
      \Alph{section}.\arabic{equation}\else
      \Alph{section}\arabic{equation}\fi}  % Comment A\arabic{equation} maybe
 \def\thetable{\ifnumbysec                 % better? 15/4/95
      \Alph{section}\arabic{table}\else
      A\arabic{table}\fi}
 \def\thefigure{\ifnumbysec
      \Alph{section}\arabic{figure}\else
      A\arabic{figure}\fi}}
\def\noappendix{\setcounter{figure}{0}
     \setcounter{table}{0}
     \def\thetable{\arabic{table}}
     \def\thefigure{\arabic{figure}}}

%
% Added redefinition of \@caption so captions are not written to 
% aux file therefore less need to \protect fragile commands
%
\long\def\@caption#1[#2]#3{\par\begingroup
    \@parboxrestore
    \normalsize
    \@makecaption{\csname fnum@#1\endcsname}{\ignorespaces #3}\par
  \endgroup}
% 
\long\def\@makecaption#1#2{\vskip \abovecaptionskip 
 \begin{indented}
 \item[]{\bf #1.} #2
 \end{indented}\vskip\belowcaptionskip}

\newcommand\@tocrmarg {2.55em}
\newcommand\@dotsep{4.5}
\setcounter{tocdepth}{3}
\newcommand\tableofcontents{%
    \section*{\contentsname
        \@mkboth{\uppercase{\contentsname}}{\uppercase{\contentsname}}}%
    \@starttoc{toc}%
    }
\newcommand\l@part[2]{%
  \ifnum \c@tocdepth >-2\relax
    \addpenalty{\@secpenalty}%
    \addvspace{2.25em \@plus\p@}%
    \begingroup
      \setlength\@tempdima{3em}%
      \parindent \z@ \rightskip \@pnumwidth
      \parfillskip -\@pnumwidth
      {\leavevmode
       \large \bfseries #1\hfil \hbox to\@pnumwidth{\hss #2}}\par
       \nobreak
       \if@compatibility
         \global\@nobreaktrue
         \everypar{\global\@nobreakfalse\everypar{}}
      \fi
    \endgroup
  \fi}
\newcommand\l@section[2]{%
  \ifnum \c@tocdepth >\z@
    \addpenalty{\@secpenalty}%
    \addvspace{1.0em \@plus\p@}%
    \setlength\@tempdima{1.5em}%
    \begingroup
      \parindent \z@ \rightskip \@pnumwidth
      \parfillskip -\@pnumwidth
      \leavevmode \bfseries
      \advance\leftskip\@tempdima
      \hskip -\leftskip
      #1\nobreak\hfil \nobreak\hbox to\@pnumwidth{\hss #2}\par
    \endgroup
  \fi}
\newcommand\l@subsection   {\@dottedtocline{2}{1.5em}{2.3em}}
\newcommand\l@subsubsection{\@dottedtocline{3}{3.8em}{3.2em}}
\newcommand\l@paragraph    {\@dottedtocline{4}{7.0em}{4.1em}}
\newcommand\l@subparagraph {\@dottedtocline{5}{10em}{5em}}
\newcommand\listoffigures{%
    \section*{\listfigurename
      \@mkboth{\uppercase{\listfigurename}}%
              {\uppercase{\listfigurename}}}%
    \@starttoc{lof}%
    }
\newcommand\l@figure{\@dottedtocline{1}{1.5em}{2.3em}}
\newcommand\listoftables{%
    \section*{\listtablename
      \@mkboth{\uppercase{\listtablename}}{\uppercase{\listtablename}}}%
    \@starttoc{lot}%
    }
\let\l@table\l@figure
\newenvironment{theindex}
               {\if@twocolumn
                  \@restonecolfalse
                \else
                  \@restonecoltrue
                \fi
                \columnseprule \z@
                \columnsep 35\p@
                \twocolumn[\section*{\indexname}]%
                \@mkboth{\uppercase{\indexname}}%
                        {\uppercase{\indexname}}%
                \thispagestyle{plain}\parindent\z@
                \parskip\z@ \@plus .3\p@\relax
                \let\item\@idxitem}
               {\if@restonecol\onecolumn\else\clearpage\fi}

\def\endTable{\end{tabular}\end{indented}\end{table}}
\let\endtab=\endTable

\def\endfulltable{\end{tabular*}\end{table}\normalsize}

\newcommand{\Bibliography}[1]{\section*{References}\par\numrefs{#1}}
\newcommand{\References}{\section*{References}\par\refs}

\def\thebibliography#1{\list
 {\hfil[\arabic{enumi}]}{\topsep=0\p@\parsep=0\p@
 \partopsep=0\p@\itemsep=0\p@
 \labelsep=5\p@\itemindent=-10\p@
 \settowidth\labelwidth{\footnotesize[#1]}%
 \leftmargin\labelwidth
 \advance\leftmargin\labelsep
 \advance\leftmargin -\itemindent
 \usecounter{enumi}}\footnotesize
 \def\newblock{\ }
 \sloppy\clubpenalty4000\widowpenalty4000
 \sfcode`\.=1000\relax}
\let\endthebibliography=\endlist
\def\numrefs#1{\begin{thebibliography}{#1}}
\def\endnumrefs{\end{thebibliography}}
\let\endbib=\endnumrefs
%
\def\thereferences{\list{}{\topsep=0\p@\parsep=0\p@
 \partopsep=0\p@\itemsep=0\p@\labelsep=0\p@\itemindent=-18\p@
\labelwidth=0\p@\leftmargin=18\p@
}\footnotesize\rm
\def\newblock{\ }
\sloppy\clubpenalty4000\widowpenalty4000
\sfcode`\.=1000\relax
}
%
\let\endthereferences=\endlist
\newlength{\indentedwidth}
\newdimen\mathindent
\indentedwidth=\mathindent
%
% Macro to used for references in the Harvard system
%
\newenvironment{harvard}{\list{}{\topsep=0\p@\parsep=0\p@
\partopsep=0\p@\itemsep=0\p@\labelsep=0\p@\itemindent=-18\p@
\labelwidth=0\p@\leftmargin=18\p@
}\footnotesize\rm
\def\newblock{\ }
\sloppy\clubpenalty4000\widowpenalty4000
\sfcode`\.=1000\relax}{\endlist}
%
\def\refs{\begin{harvard}}
\def\endrefs{\end{harvard}}
%
\newenvironment{indented}{\begin{indented}}{\end{indented}}
\newenvironment{varindent}[1]{\begin{varindent}{#1}}{\end{varindent}}
%
\def\indented{\list{}{\itemsep=0\p@\labelsep=0\p@\itemindent=0\p@
   \labelwidth=0\p@\leftmargin=\mathindent\topsep=0\p@\partopsep=0\p@
   \parsep=0\p@\listparindent=15\p@}\footnotesize\rm}

\let\endindented=\endlist 

\def\varindent#1{\setlength{\varind}{#1}%
   \list{}{\itemsep=0\p@\labelsep=0\p@\itemindent=0\p@
   \labelwidth=0\p@\leftmargin=\varind\topsep=0\p@\partopsep=0\p@
   \parsep=0\p@\listparindent=15\p@}\footnotesize\rm}

\let\endvarindent=\endlist 

\def\[{\relax\ifmmode\@badmath\else
 \begin{trivlist}
 \@beginparpenalty\predisplaypenalty
 \@endparpenalty\postdisplaypenalty
 \item[]\leavevmode
 \hbox to\linewidth\bgroup$ \displaystyle
 \hskip\mathindent\bgroup\fi}
\def\]{\relax\ifmmode \egroup $\hfil \egroup \end{trivlist}\else \@badmath \fi}
\def\equation{\@beginparpenalty\predisplaypenalty
 \@endparpenalty\postdisplaypenalty
\refstepcounter{equation}\trivlist \item[]\leavevmode
 \hbox to\linewidth\bgroup $ \displaystyle
\hskip\mathindent}
\def\endequation{$\hfil \displaywidth\linewidth\@eqnnum\egroup \endtrivlist}
%
\@namedef{equation*}{\[}
\@namedef{endequation*}{\]}
%
\def\eqnarray{\stepcounter{equation}\let\@currentlabel=\theequation
\global\@eqnswtrue
\global\@eqcnt\z@\tabskip\mathindent\let\\=\@eqncr
\abovedisplayskip\topsep\ifvmode\advance\abovedisplayskip\partopsep\fi
\belowdisplayskip\abovedisplayskip
\belowdisplayshortskip\abovedisplayskip
\abovedisplayshortskip\abovedisplayskip
$$\halign to
\linewidth\bgroup\@eqnsel$\displaystyle\tabskip\z@
 {##{}}$&\global\@eqcnt\@ne $\displaystyle{{}##{}}$\hfil
 &\global\@eqcnt\tw@ $\displaystyle{{}##}$\hfil
 \tabskip\@centering&\llap{##}\tabskip\z@\cr}
\def\endeqnarray{\@@eqncr\egroup
 \global\advance\c@equation\m@ne$$\global\@ignoretrue }
\mathindent = 6pc
%
\def\eqalign#1{\null\vcenter{\def\\{\cr}\openup\jot\m@th
  \ialign{\strut$\displaystyle{##}$\hfil&$\displaystyle{{}##}$\hfil
      \crcr#1\crcr}}\,}
%
\def\eqalignno#1{\displ@y \tabskip\z@skip
  \halign to\displaywidth{\hspace{5pc}$\@lign\displaystyle{##}$%
    \tabskip\z@skip
    &$\@lign\displaystyle{{}##}$\hfill\tabskip\@centering
    &\llap{$\@lign\hbox{\rm##}$}\tabskip\z@skip\crcr
    #1\crcr}}
%
\newif\ifnumbysec
\def\theequation{\ifnumbysec
      \arabic{section}.\arabic{equation}\else
      \arabic{equation}\fi}
\def\eqnobysec{\numbysectrue\@addtoreset{equation}{section}}

\newcounter{eqnval}

% 2012: if you have an eqn numbered by parts (eg eqn 6a, 6b) this allows
% you to refer to it by just the number (eg eqn 6) if the label is between
% the \multiparteqn and the \numparts
\def\multiparteqn{\addtocounter{equation}{1}
\eqnarray\nonumber
\endeqnarray

\vspace{-72pt}
}

\def\numparts{\addtocounter{equation}{1}%
     \setcounter{eqnval}{\value{equation}}%
     \setcounter{equation}{0}%
     \def\theequation{\ifnumbysec
     \arabic{section}.\arabic{eqnval}{\it\alph{equation}}%
     \else\arabic{eqnval}{\it\alph{equation}}\fi}}

\def\endnumparts{\def\theequation{\ifnumbysec
     \arabic{section}.\arabic{equation}\else
     \arabic{equation}\fi}%
     \setcounter{equation}{\value{eqnval}}}
%
\def\cases#1{%
     \left\{\,\vcenter{\def\\{\cr}\normalbaselines\openup1\jot\m@th%
     \ialign{\strut$\displaystyle{##}\hfil$&\tqs
     \rm##\hfil\crcr#1\crcr}}\right.}%

   \abovedisplayshortskip \z@ \@plus2\p@

\title[The Foundation of Gravitation]{The Foundation of Gravitation: Vectors, Angular Kinematics and Elements of General Relativity}
\author{Sohel Georgiadis}
\address{Student, The Reality Public School\\Kokrajhar, Assam, India}
\ead{\href{mailto:sohelgeorgiadis@gmail.com}{sohelgeorgiadis@gmail.com}}
\vspace{10pt}
\begin{indented}
\item[]21 October 2025
\end{indented}
\begin{abstract}
This exposition examines how velocity direction, conservation laws and assumptions about the source determine gravitational motion. Circular acceleration and angular momentum lead to the calculation of orbital speeds, escape conditions, Keplerian periods and rendezvous timing. The distinction between gravitational potential and potential energy is developed through exterior and interior spherical models. The altitude law requires spherical symmetry, while the linear depth law additionally requires uniform density. A velocity-Verlet calculation of an eccentricity-0.6 orbit is compared with the analytic solution. At 20,000 steps per period, the maximum relative energy error is $7.31\times10^{-7}$. Halving the time step reduces that error by approximately a factor of four over the reported runs, providing a numerical consistency check. The relativistic discussion uses the supplied Schwarzschild exterior interval and radial geodesic energy constant to calculate supported-clock rates, radial light propagation and free-fall proper time. Finite falling-clock time to the horizon is distinguished from divergent Schwarzschild coordinate time, and coordinate light speed from locally measured light speed. Algebra, geometry, vectors and single-variable calculus suffice for the calculations presented. The Schwarzschild solution is not derived from the field equations. The manuscript synthesises established results and model calculations without claiming new physical laws or observational evidence.
\end{abstract}
\vspace{-6pt}
\begin{indented}
\item[]\centering\includegraphics[width=230pt,height=133pt,keepaspectratio]{fg-earthrise-cover.pdf}\par
\vspace{4pt}
{\footnotesize Earthrise, Apollo 8, 24 December 1968. NASA/Bill Anders.}
\end{indented}

\FloatBarrier
\section{Introduction and scope}

Give two bodies the same speed at the same distance from a planet. One may follow a circle and the other an ellipse, because their velocity directions differ. Energy alone cannot distinguish them. Angular momentum supplies the missing constraint. This elementary comparison sets the problem pursued here: what information is needed to calculate a gravitational trajectory, and what may be inferred from the motion once it is known?

Circular motion is a useful starting point because it separates change of direction from change of speed. The inward acceleration identifies the force required at an instant. Torque then determines whether angular momentum is conserved, while work determines how kinetic energy changes. Under an inverse-square central force, these relations constrain the size, shape and period of an orbit. An encounter requires the two bodies to occupy the same position at the same time. A completed orbital rendezvous also requires their velocities to match.

The force law also needs a model of its source. Outside a spherical body, only the total mass enters the field. Inside it, the enclosed mass changes with radius. Potential records the work per unit test mass, including contributions from shells whose net interior force vanishes. These distinctions become necessary both when calculating a path and when using a measured path to infer mass.

The Newtonian treatment uses a common time coordinate and Euclidean space. It does not provide a law for comparing clocks held at different gravitational potentials or carried along different relativistic paths. Those questions require an interval that relates coordinate changes to local measurements. The Schwarzschild exterior supplies the specific geometry used here. Its weak-field limit recovers a relation involving Newtonian potential, but potential and spacetime curvature remain different quantities.

The calculations assume algebra, geometry, vectors and single-variable differentiation and integration. Circular acceleration, the work--energy relation, spherical field and potential profiles, and several consequences of Keplerian motion are derived. The shell theorem, the conic form of inverse-square orbits, the Schwarzschild interval and the radial geodesic energy constant are supplied results. Worked applications test the use of these relations. A numerical orbit calculation checks a particular implementation of the Newtonian model. None of these calculations substitutes for deriving the relativistic field equations or testing a gravitational theory against observations.

\subsection{Mathematical conventions}

A derivative is a local rate of change. Position changing with time gives velocity; velocity changing with time gives acceleration. Both velocity and acceleration have directions. Speed is only the magnitude of velocity.


\eqdisplay{v_x=\frac{dx}{dt},\qquad a_x=\frac{dv_x}{dt}}

An integral adds many small contributions. Work adds force along small displacements. A clock's elapsed proper time adds the small intervals that clock actually experiences.


\eqdisplay{W=\int F_x\,dx,\qquad \Delta\tau=\int\frac{d\tau}{dt}\,dt}

For vectors $\mathbf a$ and $\mathbf b$, the dot product is $\mathbf a\cdot\mathbf b=ab\cos\theta$. It selects the component along the other vector. The cross product has magnitude $|\mathbf a\times\mathbf b|=ab\sin\theta$, so it includes the perpendicular lever arm. Its direction follows the right-hand rule. For vectors in the page, that direction is into or out of the page.


A radian is arc length divided by radius. One revolution is $2\pi$ radians. Radians are dimensionless, so $v=\omega r$ has units of metres per second.


Useful constants for the worked examples are g = 9.81 m $s^{-2}$, Earth's mean radius $R_{E}$ = 6.371 $\times$ $10^{6}$ m, Earth's gravitational parameter $\mu _{E}$ = G$M_{E}$ = 3.986 $\times$ $10^{14}$ $m^{3}$ $s^{-2}$, and c = 2.998 $\times$ $10^{8}$ m $s^{-1}$. These are rounded teaching values, not precision ephemerides.

For the solar-mass and kiloparsec examples, use $GM_{\odot}=1.327\times10^{20}\ {\rm m^3\,s^{-2}}$ and $1\ {\rm kpc}=3.086\times10^{19}\ {\rm m}$. These rounded conversion values suffice to reproduce the reported estimates. \cite{P08}


\textbf{Notation.} T means period; $F_{T}$ means string tension. The symbol $\tau$ means torque in Section 3 and proper time in Section 8. Context distinguishes them. Lowercase h denotes altitude in Section 4 and specific angular momentum in orbital equations. Depth below the surface is d, with $r=R-d$. The symbol a means acceleration in Section 2 and semimajor axis in Section 6.

\section{Circular motion and perceived gravity}

\subsection{Support at the rotating rim}

Consider a person standing at the inner rim of a rotating space station, far from planets. Their path is circular even though they remain at rest relative to the floor. The floor must therefore push them inward. Their apparent weight is this support force, while the direction they call down points toward the rim.


Two arrows keep the descriptions separate. The contact force points toward the axis. The perceived direction of down points away from it. A force diagram must contain the actual contact force appropriate to the chosen frame.


\begin{figure}[htbp]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=\textwidth]{fg-01-circular-motion.pdf}
\caption{Circular motion. Left: position and velocity triangles illustrating the inward change of velocity (OpenStax, figure 4.18). Right: calculated acceleration as radius varies, with speed or angular speed held fixed; each curve is normalised at its reference radius. OpenStax diagrams: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0. Access for free at \url{https://openstax.org/books/university-physics-volume-1/pages/1-introduction} .}\label{fig:plate1}
\end{figure}

\subsection{Angular speed and tangential velocity}

At the rightmost point of a counterclockwise circle, velocity points upward. A quarter-turn later it points left. Even if the speedometer never changes, the velocity vector has changed, so acceleration exists.


For radius r and period T, one circuit covers 2$\pi$r. Frequency f counts circuits per second, while angular speed $\omega$ counts radians per second.


\eqdisplay{f=\frac{1}{T},\qquad \omega=\frac{2\pi}{T},\qquad v=\frac{2\pi r}{T}=\omega r}

All points of a rigid turntable share one angular speed $\omega$. Their speeds $v$ increase with distance from the axis. Independently orbiting bodies obey no such rigid constraint. Consequently, the radius dependence of $v^2/r$ must be evaluated with the specified quantity held fixed.


\subsection{Angular kinematics and nonuniform circular motion}

An angular coordinate specifies position around a fixed axis. Its first time derivative is angular velocity and its second is angular acceleration. In planar motion a positive sign denotes counterclockwise rotation under the chosen convention. Their units are radians per second and radians per second squared.


\eqdisplay{\omega=\frac{d\theta}{dt},\qquad \alpha=\frac{d\omega}{dt}=\frac{d^2\theta}{dt^2}}

For motion on a circle of fixed radius r, the signed tangential velocity is r$\omega$ and its tangential acceleration is r$\alpha$. The velocity direction also changes, producing an inward acceleration $r\omega ^{2}$. With outward radial unit vector $\hat{\mathbf r}$ and counterclockwise tangent $\hat{\boldsymbol\theta}$, the complete planar vectors are


\eqdisplay{\mathbf v=r\omega\hat{\boldsymbol\theta},\qquad \mathbf a=-r\omega^2\hat{\mathbf r}+r\alpha\hat{\boldsymbol\theta}}

The two acceleration components are perpendicular, so the magnitude of the total acceleration is the square root of the sum of their squares. Uniform circular motion is the special case $\alpha$ = 0; the radial component remains nonzero.


\begin{figure}[htbp]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=.40\textwidth]{fg-neutelings-radial-tangential.pdf}
\caption{Acceleration decomposition by Izaak Neutelings \cite{M05}. The total acceleration is the vector sum of perpendicular tangential and normal components. The source labels the normal component $a_c$ and the tangential component $a_t$. For a circle of fixed radius, their magnitudes are $r\omega^2$ and $r|\alpha|$. Reproduced as vector artwork under CC BY-SA 4.0.}\label{fig:plate2}
\end{figure}

When $\alpha$ is constant, integrating once gives the angular velocity and integrating again gives angular position. Eliminating time yields a third useful relation:


\eqdisplay{\omega=\omega_0+\alpha t,\qquad \theta-\theta_0=\omega_0t+\frac12\alpha t^2}

\eqdisplay{\omega^2=\omega_0^2+2\alpha(\theta-\theta_0)}

These relations require a fixed axis, a consistent angular sign convention and constant angular acceleration. For example, a rotor starting from rest with $\alpha$ = 0.4 rad $s^{-2}$ reaches 2 rad $s^{-1}$ after 5 s and turns through 5 radians. At radius 0.5 m its tangential acceleration is 0.2 m $s^{-2}$ throughout, whereas its inward acceleration reaches 2 m $s^{-2}$ at that final time. The distinct behaviour of the two components explains why a changing angular speed requires more than an inward-force condition alone.


\subsection{Derivation of centripetal acceleration}

Compare the velocity vectors at two nearby points on a circle. They have equal lengths and a small angle $\Delta$$\theta$ between them. The small triangle formed by their difference is similar to the triangle formed by the two radius vectors.


\eqdisplay{\frac{|\Delta\mathbf v|}{v}\simeq\frac{\Delta s}{r}}

Since $\Delta$s/$\Delta$t approaches v, divide by $\Delta$t and take the limit. The change in velocity points toward the centre in that limit.


\eqdisplay{a_c=\frac{v^2}{r}=\omega^2r}

The result can be checked using single-variable calculus. Write the circular trajectory as x = r cos($\omega$t), y = r sin($\omega$t). Differentiate each coordinate twice. Differentiation gives $a_{x}$ = $-$$\omega ^{2}$x and $a_{y}$ = $-$$\omega ^{2}$y: acceleration is the negative of the radius vector multiplied by $\omega ^{2}$.


If the speed changes as well, acceleration has an additional tangential component. The inward component $v^{2}$/r is still present. Uniform circular motion is the special case with zero tangential component.


\subsection{Forces producing circular motion}

The inward component of the net force must supply this acceleration. Tension, gravity, friction or a normal force may contribute. The term centripetal names the required direction of the resultant. It does not identify an additional interaction.


\eqdisplay{\sum F_{\rm inward}=\frac{mv^2}{r}}

Cutting a string removes its tension without changing the instantaneous velocity. The object initially moves along the tangent. Its subsequent path is straight if no net force remains, or curved if gravity or another force continues to act.


\subsection{A habitat with specified apparent weight}

Take a habitat of radius 100 m. Require an inward acceleration of one Earth g at its rim. Ignore the station's own gravity and the occupant's motion relative to the floor.


\eqdisplay{\omega=\sqrt{\frac{g}{r}}=0.313\ {\rm rad\ s^{-1}}}

\eqdisplay{T=\frac{2\pi}{\omega}=20.1\ {\rm s},\qquad v=\sqrt{gr}=31.3\ {\rm m\ s^{-1}}}

The rotation rate is about 2.99 revolutions per minute. For a person stationary relative to the rim, the floor supplies $N=mg$ inward. The symbol $g$ specifies the desired acceleration in this calculation. The station has produced a support force without a planetary gravitational field.


At the same angular speed, the required acceleration is proportional to distance from the axis. At 50 m it is half the rim value; at the axis it is zero. Moving around inside a rotating habitat introduces additional effects, including Coriolis deflection, beyond this stationary-occupant calculation.


If the radius is doubled while the required rim acceleration stays fixed, the angular speed falls by $\sqrt{2}$, the period grows by $\sqrt{2}$, and the rim speed grows by $\sqrt{2}$. The constraint is fixed apparent weight, not fixed rotation rate.


\subsection{Maintaining contact in a vertical circle}

At the top of a vertical circle, toward the centre is downward. Gravity points downward, and the bottom of the upside-down bucket can also push the water downward. Let N be that contact force on a representative bit of water.


\eqdisplay{mg+N=\frac{mv_{\rm top}^2}{r}}

For the stated contact model, $N$ cannot be negative. Setting $N=0$ identifies the threshold at which gravity alone supplies the inward acceleration.


\eqdisplay{v_{\rm top}\geq\sqrt{gr}}

For r = 1 m, the minimum top speed is 3.13 m $s^{-1}$. Gravity supplies the entire inward acceleration at that threshold. The result is a condition on the speed \textbf{at the top}, not an instruction to use one constant speed everywhere.


If a point mass on a taut, massless string passes through a complete vertical loop with only gravity doing work, the bottom is 2r lower. Energy conservation gives $v_{\rm bottom}^2=v_{\rm top}^2+4gr$. At the limiting top speed:


\eqdisplay{v_{\rm bottom}=\sqrt{5gr},\qquad F_{T,\rm bottom}=6mg}

The vanishing contact force at the top therefore coexists with a large tension at the bottom. Force balance gives the condition at each location. The relation between the two speeds comes from the work done during the descent, developed in Section 4.


\subsection{Acceleration in a centrifuge}

At 1,200 rpm, frequency is 20 $s^{-1}$ and $\omega$ = 40$\pi$ rad $s^{-1}$. At radius 0.15 m:


\eqdisplay{a_c=(40\pi)^2(0.15)=2.37\times10^3\ {\rm m\ s^{-2}}\simeq241g}

The result specifies the required inward force per unit mass and the corresponding effective acceleration in the rotating frame. The particle's mass is unchanged. In a liquid, separation also depends on density difference, drag, particle size and thermal motion, so the circular point-particle model supplies only part of the description.


\FloatBarrier
\section{Angular momentum and torque}

\subsection{What contraction preserves}

A skater pulling in their arms can increase both angular speed and rotational kinetic energy while the external torque remains negligible. The preceding force calculation is not enough to explain this change. We must identify the conserved quantity and distinguish it from the energy transferred during contraction.


\begin{figure}[htbp]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=\textwidth]{fg-02-angular-momentum.pdf}
\caption{Angular momentum and contraction. Left: a particle in circular motion, with position $\mathbf r$, tangential momentum $\mathbf p$ and perpendicular angular momentum $\mathbf L$ following the right-hand rule (Izaak Neutelings \cite{M05}). The circle appears elliptical in perspective. Right: calculated angular speed and rotational kinetic energy at fixed angular momentum; the normalised curves coincide. Illustration: CC BY-SA 4.0.}\label{fig:plate3}
\end{figure}

\subsection{Dependence on the chosen origin}

Choose a fixed point O in an inertial frame. For a particle, r points from O to the particle and p = mv is its momentum.


\eqdisplay{\mathbf L_O=\mathbf r\times\mathbf p,\qquad |L_O|=mvr\sin\theta=mvb}

Here b is the perpendicular distance from O to the particle's line of motion. A particle moving along a straight line can have angular momentum about a point away from that line. It does not need to follow a circle.


For a particle moving left above O, $\mathbf r\times\mathbf p$ points out of the page. If O is moved onto the line of motion, the perpendicular distance $b$ becomes zero. The motion is unchanged, but its angular momentum about the new origin is zero.


Linear momentum also depends on the reference frame. In a chosen inertial frame it does not additionally require an origin; angular momentum does.


\subsection{The torque equation}

Differentiate r $\times$ p about that fixed inertial origin. The product rule gives two terms. Since dr/dt = v and p = mv, v $\times$ p is zero.


\eqdisplay{\frac{d\mathbf L_O}{dt}=\mathbf v\times\mathbf p+\mathbf r\times\frac{d\mathbf p}{dt}=\mathbf r\times\mathbf F=\boldsymbol\tau_O}

The torque magnitude is $Fb$, where $b$ is now the perpendicular distance to the force's line of action. A push along the line from a hinge to a door handle has no moment about the hinge. A transverse push has a moment set by that perpendicular distance.


Torque and angular momentum must use the same origin. Zero torque about the centre of a planet does not automatically mean zero torque about some other point.


\subsection{Angular momentum under a central force}

Gravity from an ideal spherical central body points along the radius. Parallel or antiparallel vectors have zero cross product, so r $\times$ F = 0 about that centre. Angular momentum about the centre is conserved even on an ellipse, where speed and distance change continuously.


For a system of particles, the internal pair torques cancel when the pair forces are equal, opposite and directed along the line joining the particles. Equal and opposite forces with different lines of action can instead form a couple. With the usual central internal forces of the Newtonian particle model, the remaining torque is the total external torque.


\eqdisplay{\frac{d\mathbf L_{\rm total}}{dt}=\boldsymbol\tau_{\rm external}}

Zero external torque fixes the total vector, not necessarily each object's share of it. Components within a system can exchange angular momentum.


\subsection{Moment of inertia and axial rotation}

For rotation about a fixed symmetry axis, a mass $m_i$ at perpendicular distance $\rho_i$ has speed $\omega\rho_i$. Its axial angular momentum is $m_i\rho_i^2\omega$. Summing over the masses defines the moment of inertia.


\eqdisplay{I=\sum_i m_i\rho_i^2,\qquad L_{\rm axis}=I\omega}

Moment of inertia specifies the mass distribution relative to the axis. Equal total mass does not mean equal I. Moving mass twice as far from an axis multiplies that part's contribution by four.


The vector statement L = I$\omega$ needs the appropriate principal or symmetry axis. We do not use it as a universal rule for arbitrary three-dimensional rotation; that general problem requires more machinery than this paper assumes.


\subsection{Spin and orbital contributions}

A spinning satellite can orbit Earth. About Earth's centre, one contribution comes from the centre of mass going around Earth, and another from rotation about the satellite's own centre of mass.


\eqdisplay{\mathbf L_O=\mathbf R_{\rm cm}\times\mathbf P+\mathbf L_{\rm cm}}

The centre-of-mass term is orbital angular momentum about O. The second term is spin angular momentum about the centre of mass. Both arise from the same definition, applied to different parts of the total motion.


\subsection{The work required for contraction}

Let I change from 6 to 2 kg $m^{2}$. Initially $\omega$ = 2 rad $s^{-1}$. With negligible external torque, L = 12 kg $m^{2}$ $s^{-1}$ throughout, so the final angular speed is 6 rad $s^{-1}$.


Rotational kinetic energy is K = $I\omega ^{2}$/2. Substitute $\omega$ = L/I to see what fixed L implies.


\eqdisplay{K_{\rm rot}=\frac{L^2}{2I}}

The initial energy is 12 J and the final energy is 36 J. The additional 24 J is supplied by work during contraction, drawn from the skater's internal energy. The torque condition fixes angular momentum while leaving room for this energy transfer.


Holding $\omega$ fixed with an external motor changes the problem. Angular momentum then changes with $I$, and the motor or support exchanges torque with the system. The energy calculation must follow that new constraint.


\subsection{A contracting stellar core}

Model a collapsing stellar core as I = $kMR^{2}$. If its mass M, structural factor k, and angular momentum remain unchanged, then $\omega$ is proportional to 1/$R^{2}$ and the rotation period is proportional to $R^{2}$.


\eqdisplay{\frac{T_f}{T_i}=\left(\frac{R_f}{R_i}\right)^2}

A hypothetical core shrinking from 10,000 km to 10 km shrinks in radius by 1,000, so its period shrinks by one million. An initial 30-day period becomes about 2.59 seconds.


This estimate isolates the effect of contraction at fixed mass, structural factor and angular momentum. Real collapse can eject mass and angular momentum, change the density distribution and require relativity. The hypothetical core therefore illustrates a mechanism without predicting the final state of a particular star.


Pulsars are rapidly rotating neutron stars whose emission can sweep past us. If the beam crosses our line of sight, rotation produces pulses. Beam geometry matters: not every neutron star presents a beam to Earth.


\subsection{Limits of the compact-remnant comparison}

For compact stellar remnants, support and gravity determine what configurations are possible, while angular momentum constrains rotation during change. The detailed mass thresholds and equations of state are beyond this section.


For a black hole of nonzero mass, the horizon has a finite scale. It is distinct from the classical central singularity. A uniform material density does not define a black hole, so the preceding contraction model cannot be extrapolated into a description of its interior. Section 8 specifies the exterior model used for the relativistic calculation.
